# Quick Review



* All languages have words\, but what is a word?
  * Not really about letters and spaces…
  * It’s all about meaning\!
* Knowing a word requires:
  * Phonetic/phonological knowledge
  * Syntactic knowledge
  * Morphological knowledge
  * Semantic knowledge

---


![](images/Recitation%204_1.jpg)



* We introduced:
  * __Phonetics__  is the study of the sounds in a language
  * __Phonology __ is the study of the  _system_  of contrastive relationships among the speech sounds
  * __Syntax __ is the study of the way in which words are put together to form phrases and sentences
  * __Morphology__  is the study of word formation\, including a word’s component parts\, internal structure\, and rules for word creation
  * __Semantics__  is the study of meaning

---


# Morphemes?


---




* What does it mean that we use morphological rules to create new words?
  * Like “happy” becoming “unhappy” by adding the un\- prefix\, people invent new words all the time by simply combining materials \(morphemes\!\) already in the language
  * For example\, “Instagram” is a  __portmanteau __ \(or a kind of blending\) of the words “instant camera” and “telegram” – two old technologies that get repurposed for the photo\-sharing app
    * The creators took morphemes from those two words \(sort of…”insta\-” is weird\) and smushed them together
    * Lots of examples of portmanteaus – like?
  * But it is also how we convert the proper name “Instagram” into new kinds of words\!
    * Can you make “Instagram” into an adjective?
    * Make it fit this sentence – “That picture is so \_\_\_\_\!” or “That is an \_\_\_\_ picture\!”

# Parts of speech!



* We also revisited \(because you learned these in grade school\)  __parts of speech__ \!
  * What are these? Nouns\, Verbs\, Adjectives\, Adverbs\, Prepositions\, Pronouns
  * Sometimes classification can be fuzzy \(same form ≠ same word\) – examples?
* Not about memorizing categories
* You “know” them even if you don’t know you know them

# Activity time!



* __Mad Libs\!__
* Fill in the blanks with appropriate answers \(keep it clean\!\):
* 1\.	\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ walks the \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ dog\.
  * \(pronoun\)		     \(adjective\)
* 2\.	Students \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ this \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ at night\.
  * \(preposition\)	\(noun\)        \(verb\)
* 3\.	Her sister from Tulsa \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ a\(n\) \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\.
* \(verb\)	          \(adjective\)  \(noun\)
::: {.notes}

Let them work in groups. Have them turn in a page with their names and their answers.
Talk about words that can be fuzzy. Of the ones already here, “walks” can be a noun like “I like to go on morning walks.” How do we know it’s a verb here? What about the words they filled in? Could any of those have other meanings?
Xander found this: https://svickars.github.io/mad-libs/ 

:::

# Activity time!



* __Part II: Morphological rules__
  * What is the plural marker in Esperanto? __ __
  * What is the marking found on the object of the verb?
  * If you have a plural object of the verb\, which comes first – plural or object marking?
  * What is the third person singular marking on the verb?
  * What happens to the verb\-final vowel when you add the third person singular marking on the verb? Does it remain or get deleted?
::: {.notes}

**NOT DOING THIS ONE***
Let them work in groups. Have them turn in a page with their names and their answers to both parts of the activity.

Here is some data from Esperanto (with English translations). Look it over and answer the questions.
What is the plural marker? -j
What is the marking found on the object of the verb? -n
If you have a plural object of the verb, which comes first – plural or object marking? plural
What is the third person singular marking on the verb? –as
What happens to the verb-final vowel when you add the third person singular marking on the verb? Does it remain or get deleted? Gets deleted
